subject: Small-boat based cetacean monitoring in a relatively small area

messages.author: 4c918a5d3235174b
messages.subject: Small-boat based cetacean monitoring in a relatively small area
parts:
Hello everyone! 

I am new in distance sampling and just joined here recently.
 
I'm about to plan a small boat-based monitoring transects for cetacean in a 120 km² and 500 km² gulf area. I found out that it's not as vast as any cetacean survey area in any research publications. Is distance sampling method could be applicable in the area?

If so, one of the areas I mentioned before has some parts that less convex than the other. I've been thinking of stratifying the study area so I could generate line transects that more suits the topography (less off-effort time possibility). Is there anything I should consider when stratifying study area?

Any guidance is greatly appreciated.


Thank you!
Rama

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Small-boat based cetacean monitoring in a relatively small area
parts:
Rama

Welcome to the list and for your questions.

A study area of 60000km2  is not too small for applying distance sampling. There are examples in the literature of cetacean surveys in much smaller study areas, one arbitrary example:
  • Thomsen, F., Laczny, M. & Piper, W. A recovery of harbour porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) in the southern North Sea? A case study off Eastern Frisia, Germany. Helgol Mar Res 60, 189–195 (2006). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10152-006-0021-z
    A recovery of harbour porpoises (Phocoena phocoena) in the southern North Sea? A case study off Eastern Frisia, Germany - Helgoland Marine Research
    doi.org

There are several reasons for stratifying a study area; the situation you describe is to minimise off-effort. An example of this is shown in our online materials in this pair of slides:

https://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-course/lecturepdfs/Ch4/L4-4%20Automated%20Survey%20Design.pdf
